analysis.one_liner: Lets newly chartered banks meet capital rules over three years and eases rules for rural banks and thrifts.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced in January 2025 with one Republican cosponsor, has sat in the Senate Banking Committee with no hearing, markup, or vote ever since.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would make it cheaper and easier to start a new bank. New banks would get three years to build up to normal capital requirements, could change their approved business plans with a 30-day review in which silence counts as approval, and new rural community banks could operate at an 8% leverage ratio instead of 9% during their first three years. It would also lift a restriction that currently stops federal savings associations from making agricultural loans, and order a study on why so few new banks have been started. Its stated goal is to reverse the wave of bank closures and consolidations that has left many rural communities without a local bank.
analysis.who_benefits: The most direct beneficiaries are prospective bank founders and investors, who could open a bank with less capital held in reserve for three years and adjust their business plans more freely during that window. Federal savings associations gain a new lending authority for agricultural loans. Rural communities might benefit if new banks actually form and open in places now without one — but the bill imposes no requirement that new banks serve underserved areas.

how_it_helps.text: New banks would get a three-year phase-in to meet federal capital requirements, starting when their FDIC deposit insurance takes effect, lowering the upfront cash needed to launch a bank.

New rural community banks could operate at an 8% community bank leverage ratio during their first three years, with lower ratios allowed in the first two years, before returning to the current 9% standard.

During their first three years, new financial institutions could ask to deviate from the business plan regulators approved, and the agency would have 30 days to decide — with no answer counting as approval.
Federal savings associations would gain authority to make secured or unsecured agricultural loans, a business currently outside their statutory lending powers.

The bill's findings cite Federal Reserve research that 44 counties were 'deeply affected' by branch closures between 2012 and 2017, that 89% of them were rural, and that they had higher poverty rates, lower incomes, and a higher share of African-American residents than other rural counties.

analysis.who_pays: The cost of the looser capital standards falls on the safety cushion that protects depositors: if a thinly capitalized new bank fails, losses hit the FDIC deposit insurance fund, which is financed by assessments on other banks and, in a severe failure, ultimately backstopped by taxpayers. Existing banks would also face any new competitors that enter their markets under easier terms.

drawbacks.text: Capital requirements are the loss-absorbing cushion that keeps a failing bank from sticking depositors and the FDIC insurance fund with its losses; letting new banks operate at 8% leverage and phase in full capital over three years raises the chance a young bank fails with a thinner cushion, and the bill's own findings credit the post-crisis tightening of standards for shaping today's rules.

The 'deemed approved' provision means that if a regulator does not answer a new bank's request to change its approved business plan within 30 days, the change automatically goes through — removing a checkpoint precisely during a new bank's riskiest years.

Nothing in the bill requires new banks to open branches in the underserved rural counties it cites as its justification, so the relief could flow to founders who start banks anywhere, including markets that already have plenty of banks.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The goal — more banks in places that lost theirs — is a real problem, and modestly easier entry is a reasonable way to attempt it. But the bill addresses the problem only indirectly: it eases standards for all new banks and thrifts, with no targeting to underserved areas and no safeguard ensuring a new bank stays healthy through its startup years. The main measurable benefit goes to whoever launches a bank with less capital tied up; the main measurable risk lands on the deposit insurance fund and the depositors it protects.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate Banking Committee in January 2025, and the committee has not held a hearing or a vote on it since.

narrative.text: Senator Hyde-Smith introduced the bill on January 16, 2025, and it was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs.
The action history shows no activity after the referral — no hearing, no markup, no committee or floor vote.
One of 55 Senate Republicans has cosponsored the bill.
The 119th Congress is still in session, so the bill technically remains alive but has made no progress toward a vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, no one has gained from the bill itself, because it has not advanced. The beneficiaries of the current state of affairs are established banks, which continue to operate without new de novo competitors, and the existing regulatory framework, which remains unchanged.

for.name: Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and became its sole sponsor.

against.name: Senate Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and has taken no further action on it — no hearing, no markup, no vote.

sides.party_line_note: Both the sponsor and the sole cosponsor are Republicans, and no member of either party has voted on the bill or taken a recorded position beyond that.

industries.industry: Prospective de novo bank founders and investors
industries.note: Three years of relaxed capital requirements and fast-tracked business-plan changes would let founders start banks with less money tied up in reserves. The trade-off is a thinner cushion protecting depositors, so if a young bank fails the loss shifts to the FDIC insurance fund that other banks and ultimately taxpayers stand behind.
Thrifts would gain a new statutory authority to make secured and unsecured agricultural loans, opening a lending market to them. Farm borrowers in their areas could gain a new source of credit.

New banks entering under easier terms would compete for deposits and loans in their markets, but a healthier pipeline of new banks could also slow the closures and consolidations that have been concentrating banking into larger institutions.

industries.industry: Rural and underserved communities without local banks
industries.note: These communities are the bill's stated beneficiaries: if new banks form locally, residents gain access to branches and credit. But the bill imposes no requirement that new banks locate in underserved areas, so the benefit depends entirely on where founders choose to open.

analysis.trajectory: With one cosponsor and no committee action in the months since referral, the bill is unlikely to get a hearing or markup this Congress; bills at this stage with this level of support most often expire quietly when the Congress ends in January 2027.
